MOVE AND LOGIC INSTRUCTIONS

Move instructions allow you to transfer a word of data from one location to another in the data files of a PLC. One of the best uses for move instructions is to make copies of data before changing it. This way you have a copy of the original value before it changed...
2. Use The Programming Device 4. Consult Flow Charts
DISCUSSION
There are two move instructions used by the PLC, which are shown below. They work very similar to each other. The difference is the second one provides additional functions to the move instruction...

The logic instructions allow you to perform four Boolean operations on data in memory. Logical functions have many uses and are very easy to understand. The list below shows the four logic instructions...
Let's start by looking at the move instructions.
The Move (MOV) instruction requires a source and destination. The source can be a location in a data file or a value directly entered into the instruction.
2. Use The Programming Device 4. Consult Flow Charts
Zero - High if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign - High if result is negative, low otherwise.

The destination is the address you want to send the data to. When this instruction is evaluated, the value pointed to by the source is copied into the destination location. This instruction also modifies the arithmetic status bits...

The carry bit and overflow bit are always set low. The zero bit is set high if the data moved was zero; otherwise, it is low. The sign bit is set high if the result is negative; otherwise, it is set low.
Remember, the source can be an actual value or a location of a word in a data file. The destination must be a location of a word in a data file.
This instruction is the Masked Move (MVM) instruction. It is similar to the Move instruction with additional functionality..
2. Use The Programming Device 4. Consult Flow Charts
Zero - High if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign - High if result is negative, low otherwise.
Masked Move requires an additional parameter called the mask. The mask allows you to copy specific bits to the destination, ignoring bits that you didn't want copied to the destination.
This is an example of using a mask. Ones in the mask indicate you want to copy the data; zeros indicate you want those bits in the destination to remain unchanged.

All of these instructions modify data at bit level. In other words, each bit in the source is analyzed individually. For this reason, it is important to note that data can be entered into the PLC using different numbering systems...

This instruction is the AND instruction. It requires two sources and a destination.
2. Use The Programming Device 4. Consult Flow Charts
Zero - High if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign - High if result is negative, low otherwise.

The instruction examines each source A bit and the corresponding source B bit, then AND's them together, setting the destination bit high or low accordingly. The truth table below shows what bit values put what resultant bit in the destination...

Just as the instruction states, if source bit A and source bit B are high, the result is a high bit. This instruction also modifies the arithmetic status bits. The table below shows the settings of these bits...

This instruction is the OR instruction. Just like the AND instruction, this instruction requires two sources and a destination. Note that this instruction is also known as the Inclusive OR instruction...
2. Use The Programming Device 4. Consult Flow Charts
Zero - High if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign - High if result is negative, low otherwise.
When the bits are examined, if a bit in either source A or B is high, the corresponding bit in the destination is set high. The truth table below illustrates the OR operation.
This instruction is the Exclusive Or (XOR) instruction. Like the previous logic instructions, two sources and a destination are required.
2. Use The Programming Device 4. Consult Flow Charts
Zero - High if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign - High if result is negative, low otherwise.

The truth table below shows the conditions which cause a high bit in the destination location. If the source bits are either both high or both low, the resultant destination bit will be low. If the source bits are opposite (one high and one low), the destination bit will be high...
As with the other instructions, the XOR instruction also sets the arithmetic bits as shown below. Notice only the zero and sign bits indicate any information about the destination information.
The last instruction we will examine is the NOT instruction. Notice this instruction only requires one source and a destination.

Zero - High if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign - High if result is negative, low otherwise.
All bits in the source are inverted to the opposite value and placed in the destination.

Definition
The program shown below is the ladder logic you will enter to demonstrate some of the move and logic instructions that you learned in the first part of this lesson.
Before we begin entering the program into the PLC APS software, let's look at what the program should do. This will
help us understand if the program is operating properly when
On the 5050-1 PC card, there are three switches that we will use for this program: two push button switches and a slide switch.
The START and STOP push-buttons set the first bit of two words that will be logically evaluated. The slide switch controls which logical operation, AND or XOR.
The first rung of the ladder logic program checks to see if the START button is pushed in. If the button is pressed in, the value 0000000000000001 is moved into word B3:0.
By moving this value in, we only set the first bit to high. All the rest of the bits remain at zero. When we use the XOR and AND instructions, we will only be concerned with the first bit.

The next rung again checks the START button's condition. If the START button isn't pressed, the value 0000000000000000 is moved into B3:0. This sets the first bit to low, as the rest of the bits are set...

Rung 3 looks to see if the STOP button is pressed in. If the STOP button is pressed in, the value 0000000000000001 is moved into B3:1. Notice that this is a different word than the one used by the START button...

In Rung 4, the STOP button is not pressed in, causing the value 0000000000000000 to be moved into B3:1. You can see that the START and STOP buttons perform the same operation on two words in the binary data file...

In the next rung, we check to see if the slide switch is in the right position. If this condition is met, the value in B3:0 is ANDed with B3:1 and placed into the output as a destination. This output is the one attached to the LEDs on the PLC Trainer...
Remember, only one bit is changed in both words, so only one LED will be on or off on the PLC Trainer. The LED you will be concerned with is LED 0.

The last rung of the ladder logic program checks to see if the slide switch is in the left position. If the switch is in this position, B3:0 is XORed with B3:1 and the result is placed into the output data file, just as with the AND instruction...
The purpose of this program is to demonstrate a simple move instruction and verify the truth table destination results with the AND and XOR instructions.
The AND and XOR instructions evaluate all bits of both words; however, we set the higher bits, other than the one we are interested in, to low.
